walkthroughs.h2: What makes a good exchange surface
walkthroughs.body_html:
Exchange surfaces have a large surface area, are thin and have a good blood supply.

Alveoli have all three: millions of tiny sacs, walls one cell thick, capillary network.

Red blood cells carry O₂. White blood cells fight infection. Platelets clot. Plasma dissolves glucose, hormones, CO₂ and urea.

RBCs are biconcave, have no nucleus, and contain haemoglobin.

Right side pumps deoxygenated blood to lungs. Left side pumps oxygenated blood to body.

Blood reaches body cells at higher pressure — fast O₂ delivery for active animals.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?
options: Both move substances down a concentration gradient, but active transport is faster.
Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.
Active transport requires energy (ATP) and can move substances against the concentration gradient.

The left ventricle is thicker because it handles oxygenated blood, which is harder to pump.
It must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body; the right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs.
The left ventricle is thicker because it is on the same side as the brain.

mcqs.q: Roughly how many alveoli in a pair of lungs (millions)?
Alveoli provide a large surface area, thin walls and a good blood supply. Together these features:
options: Maximise the rate of gas exchange by diffusion
Slow down gas exchange to protect the lungs
Allow active transport of oxygen into blood
Prevent carbon dioxide from leaving the blood

mcqs.q: Why is a single-celled organism able to rely on diffusion alone for gas exchange, while a large mammal needs lungs and a blood system?
options: A large organism has a small surface area to volume ratio.
A large organism has a large surface area to volume ratio.
Single cells do not need oxygen.
Diffusion works faster over long distances.

Fights pathogens in the blood
Clots the blood at a wound
